common_name: Grey-Leaved Strelitzia (Great White Bird of Paradise)

planting.note: Divide basal offsets or plant large container specimens in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; this rare Garden Route species is more cold-sensitive than S. reginae and needs deep, sheltered planting outside frost-free zones.

directions: One of the rarest of the large tree-form Strelitzia species, restricted in the wild to sheltered gorges and riverbanks along South Africa's Garden Route. It forms a dense, multi-stemmed clump of huge, oblong, grey-green leaves that shred in wind into a feathery texture quite different from the glossier blue-green leaves of S. nicolai. Flowers are produced from near-black, beak-shaped spathes and are pure white with a white crest, larger than those of S. reginae and lacking the blue petal accents typical of S. nicolai. Best used as a dramatic single specimen in sheltered courtyards or large containers where its distinctive shredded grey foliage and stark white blooms can be appreciated up close.
sources: South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) - PlantZAfrica
Kew Science - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide rhizomes with at least one growing point or plant container-grown specimens in consistently moist, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade after frost danger has passed; this species needs rich, evenly moist conditions and warm nights to flower well.

directions: Native from Central America to northwestern Venezuela, this species produces one of the most compact and densely packed pendant inflorescences in the genus: 45 to 65 tightly overlapping, deep blood-red to dark maroon bracts arranged in two opposing rows, giving rise to the common name 'beefsteak heliconia' for their meaty coloring and texture. The boat-shaped leaves carry a distinct maroon tint along the lower midrib, setting the foliage apart from the plain green leaves of H. rostrata and H. bihai. Unlike the widely spaced, dangling bracts of H. rostrata, the bracts here are held close together in a dense, compact pendant cluster. Best grown as a shaded specimen where the heavy hanging clusters can be viewed from below.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring once soil has warmed in full sun to part shade; this compact psittacorum cultivar establishes and flowers quickly, blooming nearly continuously through the warm season.

directions: A compact, heavy-blooming psittacorum cultivar distinguished by bright red bracts that fade to orange under a frosty, waxy bloom, held on slender upright stems well above narrow cane-like foliage. It tolerates more direct sun than most heliconias and flowers from spring through late autumn, drawing hummingbirds and butterflies to the small tubular true flowers nestled within each bract. Its neat, upright, clumping habit and smaller stature compared to the H. psittacorum x spathocircinata hybrids make it a popular choice for mixed tropical borders, mass plantings, and the cut-flower trade.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension - Heliconia production guide

planting.note: Sow fresh seed or set out young plants after frost danger passes in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; unlike other Ensete this species tolerates rocky, exposed sites and brief drought, and it is strictly monocarpic, dying after its one flowering and fruiting cycle.

directions: Native to rocky outcrops and cliffs of India's Western Ghats and adjacent hill ranges, this species is far more drought- and heat-tolerant than the glaucous-leaved E. glaucum or the lush E. ventricosum, thriving in barren, sharply drained sites where other bananas fail. It forms a swollen, bulb-like pseudostem base up to 8 feet in circumference topped with bright, plain green leaves lacking the powdery blue-white bloom of E. glaucum. The seeds and pseudostem have a long history of use in traditional Indian medicine. Grow as a bold architectural accent in full sun in well-drained rock gardens or raised beds rather than the moist, rich conditions typical Ensete species demand.
sources: Kew Science - Plants of the World Online
IUCN Red List of Threatened Species

planting.note: Set out rhizome divisions after all frost danger has passed into rich, moisture-retentive soil with room to roam; this wild banana spreads by a long-traveling rhizome that can send up new pseudostems several feet from the parent plant, so give it generous, unobstructed space.

directions: Known as the 'walking banana' for its unusually long, traveling rhizome, which can push up new pseudostems two meters or more from the mother plant rather than clustering tightly like most Musa species. Native to subtropical forests from northeast India through southern China and into Southeast Asia, it is valued by collectors both as a striking cold-tolerant foliage banana and as a disease-resistant wild relative used in banana breeding research. Its tender inner pseudostem core is harvested and eaten locally, though the species is grown ornamentally in Gulf Coast gardens primarily for its bold upright foliage and cold resilience rather than for fruit, which is seedy and inedible.
sources: ProMusa - Improving the understanding of banana
PMC - Whole genome sequencing of Musa itinerans
